The FOMC’s 25 bp cut to 1.50–1.75% alongside bill purchases and repo operations is a mildly dovish signal that aims to offset weak business investment/exports and below-target inflation while sustaining a strong labor market. This stance aligns with Svensson’s inflation-targeting and forecast-targeting view that policy should ease when inflation expectations and market-based inflation compensation are low to steer inflation back toward target. Evidence from Sims (1992) shows that expansionary monetary policy tends to raise real activity in the near term, and work in the spirit of Christiano and Eichenbaum (1992b) underscores short-run real effects of monetary shocks through nominal rigidities, supporting the Committee’s action to stabilize output and employment. Survey-based measures (e.g., Bullard’s emphasis on surveys) being little changed yet low inflation compensation suggest anchored but subdued expectations, reinforcing the case for accommodation but also cautioning against over-optimism. Net effect: modestly positive for the outlook and risk assets, tempered by ongoing uncertainties and dissenting votes.
